_comment: Curated selection from the Library of Congress National Jukebox. 'category' and 'note' are curator annotations written for this project (not LoC text); all other metadata is pulled from the LoC JSON API by scripts/01_fetch_loc.py.

items.note: Vess L. Ossman was the most-recorded banjoist of the acoustic era; this is an early Victor recording of a ragtime banjo solo.

Caruso's first Victor session (New York, 1 February 1904) included this aria from Leoncavallo's Pagliacci, accompanied on piano. His Victor recordings helped make the phonograph respectable for classical music.
George M. Cohan's song from the 1904 Broadway musical Little Johnny Jones, recorded in Philadelphia the following year.
Bert Williams, a Black star of vaudeville and later the Ziegfeld Follies, sings a song from Abyssinia (1906), the Williams and Walker musical named in the LoC record.
Geraldine Farrar sang Cio-Cio-San in the Metropolitan Opera's first production of Madama Butterfly (1907), the same year as this recording.
Australian soprano Nellie Melba's aria from Puccini's La Bohème, recorded in New York in 1907 for Victor's premium Red Seal series.
'Take Me Out to the Ball Game' (Norworth/Von Tilzer) was published in 1908; this Columbia recording was made the same summer.
'Red Wing' (Kerry Mills and Thurland Chattaway, 1907) was one of the most popular 'intermezzo' songs of its day; here a male duet with orchestra.
The sextet from Donizetti's Lucia di Lammermoor, sung by a Metropolitan Opera ensemble led by Caruso; Victor sold it as a premium-priced disc.
Irving Berlin's 1911 hit, recorded by the comic duo Arthur Collins and Byron Harlan within months of publication.
'Let Me Call You Sweetheart' (Friedman/Whitson, 1910) in a male-quartet arrangement typical of the period.
Scottish music-hall star Harry Lauder sings one of his signature songs; LoC files it under descriptive specialties and ethnic music.
A Peerless Quartet ragtime song from the height of the pre-war ragtime song craze.

James Reese Europe's Society Orchestra accompanied the dancers Vernon and Irene Castle. Its 1913-14 Victor sessions are among the first recordings by a Black American orchestra; LoC also credits Ford T. Dabney as composer.
W. C. Handy's 'Memphis Blues' (published 1912) sung by Morton Harvey; often cited as one of the earliest vocal recordings of a published blues.
'Poor Butterfly' (Hubbell/Golden) came from the 1916 Hippodrome revue The Big Show.
The Original Dixieland Jazz Band's 'Livery Stable Blues' (Victor, 1917) is widely regarded as the first commercially issued jazz record.
W. C. Handy's own orchestra recorded for Columbia in New York in September 1917, seven months after the ODJB's Victor version of the same tune.
George M. Cohan's First World War anthem 'Over There', sung by vaudeville star Nora Bayes in 1917.
'Tiger Rag', one of the ODJB's best-known numbers, recorded in New York in March 1918.
Enrico Caruso's 1918 recording of 'Over There', sung partly in French, shows an opera star taking on a popular war song.
Ben Selvin's 'Dardanella' was one of the best-selling dance records of the era.
George Gershwin's 'Swanee' became his first major hit after Al Jolson took it up in 1919-20.
'Whispering' (1920) was a major hit. LoC credits the Ambassador Orchestra and lists Paul Whiteman as leader, with Ferde Grofé (piano, arranger) and Henry Busse (trumpet).
The ODJB's 1921 recording of W. C. Handy's 'St. Louis Blues', with a vocal by Al Bernard according to the LoC record.
Arthur Pryor's Band, led by Sousa's former trombone soloist, plays a 'barn dance' arrangement of 'Shine On, Harvest Moon', the Nora Bayes and Jack Norworth hit of 1908.

Recorded in Mexico City in July 1905 during one of Victor's recording trips to Mexico. 'El jarabe tapatío' is the Jalisco folk dance that became Mexico's best-known national dance; here sung by Leopoldo Picazo and Jesús Abrego with guitar.

A Mexico City recording from July 1907 by Jesús Abrego (tenor) and Leopoldo Picazo (baritone), who made many guitar-accompanied duet records for Victor in 1905 and 1907. LoC also titles it 'Danza tapatía'.

'Lindas mexicanas', a march by the band's conductor V. M. Presa, played by the Mexico City Police Band (Banda de Policía de México), which recorded marches, waltzes and overtures for Victor in July 1907.
A Havana recording from February 1909. LoC lists it as a male vocal duet with guitar; the title refers to a clave, a choral song form popular in early 20th-century Havana.
Martín Silveira sings a guajiro (rural Cuban) song with bandurria accompaniment, recorded in Havana in March 1907.
The orchestra of Enrique Peña, a Havana danzón band leader, recorded in Havana in February 1909.
The Habanera from Bizet's Carmen, sung by mezzo-soprano Eleanora de Cisneros on a Columbia disc recorded in Milan. LoC gives only the year (1908) for this session.
'Ciribiribin' (Pestalozza, 1898) was one of the most popular Italian songs of the period; here a female-male duet recorded in Milan for Columbia (LoC gives only the year).
An Irish ballad recorded in London for Columbia. LoC gives only the year (1912) for this session.
The Regimental Band of H.M. Scots Guards recorded in London for Columbia (LoC gives only the year, 1911).

'Cara sucia' is an early tango title, credited by LoC to Francisco Canaro. Ignacio Riverol sings with the Orquesta Típica Loduca, whose players listed by LoC include Osvaldo Fresedo on bandoneón; recorded in Buenos Aires in May 1917.
'Torna a Surriento' (De Curtis) sung by Lia Bianca, recorded in Buenos Aires in March 1910 for the city's large Italian-speaking audience.
A gaita (Galician bagpipe) solo with drum, recorded in Buenos Aires in January 1912, reflecting the city's Galician immigrant community.
A female duet with guitar recorded in Lima in September 1913, during Victor's recording sessions in Peru.
A vocal duet with guitar and cajón (the Afro-Peruvian box drum), recorded in Lima in September 1913.
A cueca, Chile's national dance, by a vocal and instrumental group recorded in Santiago in June 1917.
Haydée Germaine sings with guitar, recorded in Santiago in June 1917.
Cezar Nunes' 'Imitação d'um batuque africano' (imitation of an African batuque), recorded in Rio de Janeiro in November 1907.
Oscar Veiga sings with violão (Brazilian guitar), recorded in Rio de Janeiro in April 1912.
'Wabash Blues' was one of the biggest dance hits of 1921; this version was recorded in Chicago in September 1921.
'Ain't We Got Fun' (Whiting/Kahn, 1921) by the Benson Orchestra of Chicago, recorded in Chicago in April 1921.
'Le rêve' from Massenet's Manon, sung by tenor Léon Beyle of the Opéra-Comique, recorded in Paris (LoC gives only the year, 1908).
'La donna è mobile' in French ('Comme la plume au vent') sung by Léon Campagnola, recorded in Paris in July 1911.
Tomás R. Abreu sings with guitar, recorded in Caracas in January 1917.
The Orquesta Típica Venezolana recorded in Caracas in February 1917.
A female vocal quartet with violin, recorded in San Juan, Puerto Rico, in January 1917.
The Orquesta Tizol recorded in San Juan in January 1917.
The Shepherd's Song and Pilgrims' Chorus from Wagner's Tannhäuser, sung by soprano Gertrud Runge with male chorus, recorded in Berlin in September 1911.
A Tokiwazu-bushi narrative song sung by Kin'nosuke with shamisen, recorded in Tokyo for Victor; LoC gives only the year (1902).
A gidayū (jōruri) excerpt from the puppet-theatre play 'Tsubosaka-dera', sung by Toyotake Roshō with shamisen, recorded in Osaka. LoC credits William C. Gaisberg as recordist.

'Caro nome' from Verdi's Rigoletto (LoC also gives the Russian title 'Vnemlya imeni ego'), sung by soprano M. A. Michailova with orchestra conducted by Bruno Seidler-Winkler; recorded in St. Petersburg by Franz Hampe. LoC gives only the year (1905).

'Zabity nezhniya lobzanya' ('Tender embraces forgotten', as LoC translates it), a Russian romance sung by baritone I. Kartaschoff with piano, recorded in St. Petersburg by Franz Hampe (LoC gives only the year, 1908).
The duet from the zarzuela 'El dúo de La Africana', with baritone Emilio Sagi-Barba, a leading zarzuela singer, and orchestra conducted by Pascual Marquina; recorded in Madrid in January 1915.
The minuet from Haydn's 'Military' Symphony (No. 100), arranged for the Royal Halberdier Guards Band of Madrid; recorded in February 1909.
A bambuco by Alejandro Wills, who sings and plays guitar, with Alberto Escobar on tiple (the Colombian treble guitar) and pito; recorded in Bogotá in November 1913.
A bambuco by Jorge A. Rubiano, sung as a male duet with guitar and tiple by his Quinteto Rubiano; recorded in Bogotá in November 1913.
A pasillo by Jorge A. Rubiano, played by the Cuarteto Nacional with Rubiano on bandurria and Alberto Escobar on tiple; recorded in Bogotá in November 1913.
'Las golondrinas', a danza, sung by soprano María Terán de Peralta with guitar; recorded in Guayaquil in October 1917.
A sanjuanito played on the rondador, the Andean panpipe, by Manuel Jesús Calle ('El Cieguito'); recorded in Guayaquil in October 1917.
A paso doble by L. Borja played by Cortes y Safadí: Vidal Moisés Cortés on tiple and Nicasio Safadí on guitar; recorded in Guayaquil in October 1917.
A pasacalle sung by Jorge Schultze (tenor) and Moisés Alurralde (baritone, guitar); recorded in La Paz in July 1917.
The 'Marcha General Pando' by S. Aranibar, played by the Orquesta Salazar under Juan Cristin Salazar; recorded in La Paz in July 1917.
'Mariposas' by Luis Duncker Lavalle, who accompanies soprano Irene Quesada on piano; recorded in Arequipa, southern Peru, in August 1917.
Riley Puckett, a blind singer and guitarist from Georgia, recorded 'Casey Jones' for Columbia in Atlanta in March 1924, during the early years of commercial country (then 'old-time') recording.
Riley Puckett sings with guitar and fiddle accompaniment, recorded in Atlanta in March 1924.
'Strawberries', a yodeling song with Riley Puckett on guitar (LoC also lists Fred Wilson as a vocalist), recorded in Atlanta in March 1924.

Warner's Seven Aces (also issued as the Corona Dance Orchestra), an Atlanta dance band led by Byron H. Warner, play McHugh and Mills's 'When My Sugar Walks Down the Street'; recorded in Atlanta in January 1925.
The Art Landry Orchestra recorded 'Rip Saw Blues' in Oakland in June 1924, during Victor's West Coast sessions.
Henry Halstead's orchestra, recorded in Oakland in June 1924.
Violinist Max Dolin with A. Schwarzmann at the piano, recorded in Oakland in January 1925.
Art Hickman's Orchestra, a pioneering San Francisco dance band, here led by Earl Burtnett; recorded 'Mandalay' in Los Angeles in June 1924.
The Montmartre Orchestra, recorded in Los Angeles in June 1924.
Earl Burtnett's orchestra, recorded in Los Angeles in June 1924.
Dave Silverman's orchestra plays 'Blue Grass Blues', recorded in St. Louis in November 1923.
The St. Louis Symphony Orchestra under Rudolph Ganz plays Sinding's 'Rustle of Spring', recorded in St. Louis in October 1923.
The St. Louis Symphony Orchestra under Rudolph Ganz plays Eduard Lassen's 'Festival Overture', recorded in St. Louis in October 1923.
Jean Goldkette's orchestra, the leading Detroit dance band of the 1920s, recorded in Detroit in March 1924.
Jean Goldkette's orchestra plays 'It's the Blues', recorded in Detroit in March 1924.
The Coon-Sanders Original Nighthawk Orchestra, famous from late-night radio broadcasts in Kansas City, with vocals by Carleton Coon and Joe Sanders; recorded in Kansas City in April 1924.
The Coon-Sanders Original Nighthawk Orchestra with Carleton Coon and Joe Sanders singing, recorded in Kansas City in April 1924.
Part 1 of Gershwin's 'Rhapsody in Blue', recorded acoustically by Paul Whiteman's orchestra with George Gershwin at the piano in New York in June 1924, four months after the premiere.

Bessie Smith's first record, 'Down Hearted Blues', recorded for Columbia in New York in February 1923 with Clarence Williams at the piano; it became one of the best-selling blues records of the decade.
Vernon Dalhart's 'Wreck of the Old 97' (Victor, 1924), with Carson Robison on guitar, was one of the first country recordings to become a national hit.
Wendell Hall accompanies himself on ukulele in his own 'It Ain't Gonna Rain No Mo'', recorded in New York in October 1923; it was a major hit of 1923-24.
'Yes! We Have No Bananas' (Silver/Cohn, 1923), the novelty hit of 1923, sung by Furman and Nash.
Fletcher Henderson's orchestra, the leading Black dance orchestra in New York in the 1920s, recorded 'Dicty Blues' in September 1923.
Fletcher Henderson's orchestra plays 'Manda' from Eubie Blake's 1924 musical 'The Chocolate Dandies', recorded in New York in October 1924.
Blues singer Maggie Jones, recorded in New York in December 1924; LoC credits Louis Armstrong on cornet and Fletcher Henderson on piano.
Frank Westphal's orchestra plays 'Stack o' Lee Blues', based on a famous ballad, recorded in Chicago in October 1923.
Art Kahn's orchestra plays 'Sobbin' Blues', recorded in Chicago in October 1923.
Ted Lewis and his band, recorded in Chicago in December 1923.
The tango 'Snobismo' by Juan Carlos Cobián, played by the Orquesta Típica of bandoneón player Osvaldo Fresedo; recorded in Buenos Aires in May 1922.
An 'aire provinciano' sung by Néstor Feria and Ítalo Goyeche with four guitars, including Enrique Maciel; recorded in Buenos Aires in March 1922.
Chilean composer Osmán Pérez Freire sings his own estilo 'El gaucho vencido' with piano, recorded in Buenos Aires in June 1922.
A son oriental (LoC also labels it a rumba) by trova guitarist Alberto Villalón, sung by Pedro Martínez and Juan de la Cruz; recorded in Havana in March 1923.
A 'son alegre' sung by the Cuarteto Cruz, a male vocal quartet with guitar and orchestra; recorded in Havana in March 1923.
A bolero by Eusebio Delfín, who sings and plays guitar in duet with Rita Montaner, later one of Cuba's most famous singers; recorded in Havana in March 1923.
A son abajeño sung by the duo Quiroz y Muñoz with guitar, recorded in Mexico City in March 1923.
Eduardo Migliaccio ('Farfariello'), the star of Italian-American vaudeville in New York, sings 'Yes! We Have No Bananas' in his own version, recorded in Camden in July 1923.
